https://www.dw.com/en/fact-check-false-v.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5MsE4 Germany's postal voting system is a frequent target for disinformation Image: Caro Kadatz/picture alliance Advertisement Berliners will vote in state and district elections on September 20 . In the days leading up to the vote, a video circulated on social media that allegedly shows a man opening postal voting envelopes and destroying ballots cast for the far-right party Alternative for Germany (AfD) . DW Fact check reviewed more than a dozen posts sharing the footage. The posts use similar captions, presenting the video as evidence of election fraud in Germany. Several have amassed hundreds of thousands of views on X. How widely has the video spread? And is its reach driven by genuine public interest? Or is something else boosting its visibility? DW Fact check investigated the video and the accounts sharing it. Claim: A video shows a man destroying AfD ballots in Berlin with a carpet knife. One post sharing the footage claims: "A video circulating in Berlin shows a man opening mail-in voting envelopes and destroying ballots marked for the AfD, while ballots for Chancellor Friedrich Merz's CDU are left intact. The footage appeared days after the AfD's landslide victory in Saxony-Anhalt. Berlin holds its state election on September 20." The post had received about 327,000 views when DW Fact Check reviewed it on September 18. According to Berlin's state returning officer, the election papers shown in the viral video are not authentic Image: X DW Fact check: False At first glance, the ballot paper appears authentic. Its names and layout match those of the official ballot paper for the Spandau 2 constituency in western Berlin, which is publicly available online . However, there are several inconsistencies in the documents shown in the video. Berlin's state returning officer, Stephan Bröchler, told DW that the documents shown in the video are not authentic election papers from Berlin. Bröchler said the envelopes shown in the video did not match the official ones used for this election. Bröchler also noted that the way the envelopes are sealed appears suspicious. According to official guidelines issued by Berlin's election authorities, postal voters receive a voting package containing a "Wahlschein," or a voter declaration that needs to be signed, plus two envelopes and the ballot papers for the elections. For the September 20 vote, Berliners receive two ballot papers: a grey-and-blue ballot for the election to the city-state House of Representatives and an orange ballot for their District Assembly. In the video, however, the documents do not correspond to the official postal voting package. The person in the video opens a red envelope and removes a white envelope. The signed voter declaration is missing. Without it, a mail-in ballot would be invalid. The person then takes out only the grey-and-blue ballot paper for the Berlin House of Representatives from the white envelope. Although voters may choose to vote in only one of the two elections, it would be unusual for three envelopes in succession to contain only one ballot paper. However, the footage does not clearly show whether the second envelope is really empty. The orange Berlin ballot paper is missing in the video circulating online Image: Caro Kadatz/picture alliance Another detail raises doubts about the video's authenticity: In the background, large grey bins allegedly containing postal ballots are marked with a version of Berlin's coat of arms featuring the Berlin bear. Bröchler said such features were not used by Berlin's election authorities. "Marking the ballot boxes with a Berlin bear is also unknown and uncommon here," he said. Bröchler's conclusion is clear: "It can be ruled out that any actual Berlin election documents are involved. The video is clearly intended to discredit postal voting." Has the video really gone viral? One of the accounts that shared the video has previously come under scrutiny. An investigation by the Lithuania-based research organization Debunk linked the account to the so-called "Sprinter" network, a group of X accounts. The researchers identified what they described as signs of coordinated and inauthentic activity, including unusually high posting volumes, frequent account renaming and evidence of purchased followers. Debunk said the network was used to amplify pro-Kremlin narratives. DW Fact check reviewed more than 15 other posts sharing the footage, many of them using nearly identical captions. Together, the posts had accumulated more than 3.2 million views by the time DW Fact check examined them. The accounts sharing the video also showed several suspicious characteristics. Almost all of the 15 accounts examined exhibited at least one sign of potentially inauthentic behavior, including rapid follower growth, frequent username changes or limited evidence of normal user engagement. One account , which presented itself as an independent media company based in West Asia, had more than 43,000 followers despite having been created only in April 2026. During that period, the account changed its username nine times. On their own, these characteristics do not prove that the accounts are coordinated or that the video's engagement was entirely artificially generated. They do, however, show that the video's apparent reach should not automatically be interpreted as evidence of widespread, organic discussion on X. A pattern seen before The video resembles other false election-related claims that have circulated about Germany in recent months. Fact check: Fake campaign about alleged division of Germany To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video Ahead of the September 6 election in the eastern state of Saxony-Anhalt, DW Fact check examined a video that similarly purported to show AfD postal ballots being destroyed. The claim was false. Among other inconsistencies, all three crossed-out ballots shown in the footage carried the same name on the signed voter declaration. The envelopes had already been opened, and the ballots lacked a hole punch required for use with voting templates designed for blind and visually impaired voters. DW Fact check has also investigated and debunked numerous other false claims targeting Germany's postal voting system . Julia Smirnova, who investigates influence operations as a researcher at the Berlin-based Center for Monitoring, Analysis and Strategy (CeMAS), told DW that these similarities, together with the way the new video is being disseminated, indicate that it is "highly likely" to be part of the Storm-1516 influence operation. German security authorities and researchers have attributed Storm-1516 to Russia. The operation has previously used fabricated videos, forged documents and purported eyewitness accounts to spread false narratives about elections and other political issues. In February 2025, Germany's Interior Ministry said it had indications that two fake videos alleging manipulation of AfD ballots were connected to the Storm 1516 campaign, citing similarities in their content and distribution. https://www.bursa.ro/education-minister-.text: The Minister of Education and Research, Mihai Dimian, rejects the image of "chaos in education" circulated in the public space and claims that the existing difficulties must be viewed in the context of the size and complexity of the system. In a post on Facebook, the minister states that over 97% of schools organized simulations for the National Assessment in the first stage, while the educational projects in the PNRR and the Baccalaureate exam were, in his opinion, examples in which fears regarding the emergence of "chaos" were not confirmed. Dimian states that since the first day of his mandate, he encountered the image of "chaos in education" in the public space, starting from the information according to which approximately half of the schools would not organize simulations for the National Assessment. The minister says that instead of giving up on organizing the simulations, he chose to dialogue with union representatives, teachers and students and prepared, together with his team, measures adapted to the situation. According to Mihai Dimian, the result was different from the scenarios initially circulated: over 97% of schools organized the simulations in the first stage, and a second stage allowed the participation of another approximately 1.5% of schools. "However, I prefer this "boring' reality, built through work, facts and results, instead of spectacular scenarios about what is about to happen,” says the minister. *PNRR and Baccalaureate, cited as examples Mihai Dimian also recalls other situations in which, he claims, major problems in education were anticipated. Among these is the implementation of the PNRR projects for education, which the minister says is approaching completion with good results, following the efforts of those involved. Another example is the Baccalaureate exam. Dimian states that it ended with "the best results in the last decade”, given that there were warnings about the emergence of major problems. The minister, however, emphasizes that the existence of problems in the system should not be denied. "There are problems in education. Some are old, others are newer, but equally serious and I have no intention of minimizing them. But problems are not synonymous with chaos”, states Mihai Dimian. *A system with over 300,000 employees In his argument, the minister emphasizes the size of the education system. The Ministry of Education and Research coordinates, according to data presented by Dimian, over 6,000 credit officers, approximately half of the total number of credit officers in the Romanian Government. The system includes over 300,000 employees, more than a quarter of all employees in public institutions and authorities, as well as approximately 3.5 million children and young people in pre-university and university education. If parents are included, the minister estimates that more than half of Romania's population is directly involved in the education system. At the same time, the Ministry is involved in the implementation of approximately 7,000 projects financed by the PNRR, representing about a third of the total number of PNRR projects carried out in Romania. "In a system of such size and complexity, in which millions of people interact daily, there will be problems, dissatisfactions or situations that need to be corrected every day,” says Dimian. *"We don't need to predict hurricanes with every flap of our wings” The minister uses the "butterfly effect,” a concept associated with complex systems theory, to explain why a specific problem should not automatically be transformed into a prediction of the collapse of the entire system. "There are enough real problems in education that we need to solve. However, we don't need to predict hurricanes with every flap of our wings,” says Dimian. He argues that the education reform cannot be achieved in a short period, but the system can be improved through continuity and consistently applied measures. "Education cannot be rebuilt in a month or a year. But it can be corrected, if we have continuity, understanding and patience," the minister also says. The structure of the school year maintains the organization by modules, separated by vacation intervals. The first break will take place between October 24 and November 1, 2026, after the end of the first learning module. The winter vacation is scheduled for December 23, 2026 - January 10, 2027, and the activity will resume on January 11, 2027. The mobile vacation in February, which will be established by each county school inspectorate and the School Inspectorate of Bucharest Municipality. This will be scheduled, depending on the decision of the local authorities, between February 15 and March 7, 2027, after consulting students, parents and teachers. The spring break is scheduled between April 24 and May 4, 2027, and will Summer camp begins after the end of classes, depending on the category of students each class is in. The last day of classes will be Friday, June 18, 2027, for most students. Articol despre School, students, teachers, year.

Photograph: Raymond Boyd/Getty Images FBI FBI says it thwarted terrorist attack in Minnesota by an 18-year-old it supplied with an AK-47 Authorities say they arrested an 18-year-old who was planning a shooting attack at the Mall of America Auzzy Byrdsell and agencies Wed 7 Oct 2026 16.27 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google FBI officials stopped a potential terrorist attack on the Mall of America in Bloomington, Minnesota , authorities announced Wednesday. An 18-year-old was arrested on one count of obtaining a firearm to carry out an act of terrorism. Sheikhdoon Abdullahi Mohamud had been investigated over the last nearly two years by the FBI. He was arrested Tuesday in a public park after he paid $600 to an undercover FBI employee posing as a member of the Islamic State for an AK-47 and 200 rounds of ammunition, according to the criminal complaint. His messages with a confidential informant revealed Mohamud expressed intent to join terrorist organizations overseas but those plans soon became a planned attack in Minnesota when those plans failed. The messages date back as far as December 2024. Mohamud was seen on the mall’s security cameras walking around “nonchalantly” and eventually robbing a Lids store at gunpoint before being apprehended, according to Minnesota police. “I wanna get martyred inshallah,” he said in the messages with the informant. “That’s why I wanna save up to go to another country or…get a gun here and just start killing a bunch of white ppl.” Daniel Rosen, a US attorney, said Mohamud “needed to be watched”. It’s unclear what initially promoted the FBI’s investigation. According to Rosen, agents “were able to detect a threat, and disrupt it, before the defendant carried out his intention to kill, in his words, maybe 30 to 60 people, as we allege in far greater detail in the complaint”. The potential shooting at the mall comes after two recent shootings by Somali teens as victims and suspects, including a gang-related shooting in Bloomington where more than 100 rounds of ammunition were fired. As terrorism and violence are an increasing concern in Minnesota, some in law enforcement are calling for a regional taskforce to address more harm in the state. Europe Cost To Living Protest Latest News Today: Growing frustration over household expenses and declining affordability has brought demonstrators onto the streets in four European countries, with protests in France, Belgium, Italy and Portugal exposing mounting pressure on governments to respond to public concerns. Saturday’s rallies reflected a range of grievances, from rising rents and low pay to university costs and anxiety over future employment. While many participants joined peaceful marches, violent incidents in several cities resulted in arrests, injured police officers and damage to public buildings and businesses. Advertisement France bore the brunt of the unrest. The country’s Interior Ministry estimated that more than 550,000 people participated in demonstrations nationwide, making it the largest mobilisation among the countries affected. The gatherings, which followed weeks of student-led protests, became increasingly disorderly in several locations. Groups of masked individuals were accused of attacking police, setting fires and breaking into shops and supermarkets. Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu said the authorities had arrested around 1,200 people, while 150 police officers sustained injuries. During a visit to officers stationed in central Paris, he described the scale of the violence as serious. Advertisement Commercial areas were affected in Paris and cities including Marseille, Nice, Nantes, Bordeaux, Limoges, Lille, Toulouse and Strasbourg. Paris Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire said the destruction had left extensive damage across parts of the capital. In Limoges, flames severely damaged the town hall, a landmark more than 140 years old. Municipal premises in Marseille and Lille were reportedly entered and vandalised, while Lyon’s tourist office was set on fire. President Emmanuel Macron said those involved in the violence would face legal consequences. Advertisement Belgium's student unrest adds to pressure In Brussels, demonstrations continued amid an existing dispute over university registration fees. Police deployed tear gas and water cannon after accusing some protesters of throwing objects at officers and starting fires. Authorities in Liège also used water cannon to disperse demonstrators. No official attendance figures were immediately available for either city. The unrest highlights how concerns about education costs are intersecting with broader economic worries, particularly among younger people facing uncertainty about their financial future. Advertisement Housing affordability dominates Portugal demonstrations Lisbon saw a large turnout, with tens of thousands of people reportedly protesting against high living costs, weak wages and the difficulty of finding affordable accommodation. Portugal’s housing market has become a major source of public concern. Property prices have more than doubled since 2017, while rents for new contracts have climbed sharply, increasing the burden on people seeking homes in major cities. The government has faced criticism for its response. Parliamentary Affairs Minister Carlos Abreu Amorim said the administration would not be dictated to by street protests. Demonstrators, however, argued that political leaders were failing to grasp the financial pressures affecting ordinary residents. Milan clashes overshadow march against war and hardship In Italy, a march in Milan that began peacefully deteriorated into confrontations between masked protesters and riot police. Demonstrators reportedly hurled stones and paving blocks, while barricades made from tables were set alight. Police used tear gas and water cannon to clear crowds from the city centre, including the area around Piazza del Duomo and a luxury shopping arcade. According to the Italian news agency LaPresse, two officers were injured and approximately 50 demonstrators were detained, many of them minors. Further clashes were reported in Bologna, where some participants in demonstrations threw stones at police. Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni condemned the destruction, saying the freedom to protest could not justify violence. Milan Mayor Giuseppe Sala acknowledged the legitimacy of concerns about living costs but said attacks on officers and damage to the city were unacceptable. Analysts warn of further mobilisation The unrest has raised the possibility that similar demonstrations could emerge elsewhere in Europe. Alberto Alemanno, a professor of European Union law and policy at HEC Paris Business School, told Al Jazeera that France remained the main centre of the current protests, although signs of discontent were appearing beyond its borders. He pointed to early signs of mobilisation in Greece, Germany and Austria and suggested that further demonstrations could take place in the coming week. Alemanno said the protests were not part of one centrally organised movement. Rather, they reflected separate campaigns driven by overlapping frustrations, including the cost of living, education funding and limited confidence in employment opportunities after graduation. The demonstrations also arrive at a politically sensitive moment, with national elections due in Spain, France, Italy and Poland over the next 12 months. The scale of public dissatisfaction could put economic policy and the cost of living at the centre of electoral debate. European leaders now face growing pressure to address the issues driving public anger, while preventing further clashes and damage as demonstrations continue to test the authorities' response.
